entries.title: drop the stale 0.18.0 platform entries from package-lock.json
entries.body: The 0.19.0 release bumped the optional platform packages in package.json but left their 0.18.0 entries in the lockfile, so `npm ls --package-lock-only` in CI's lint job failed on main and on every pull request cut from it. This is the lockfile `npm install` writes for the current package.json: stale entries removed, nothing added.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: count the resets an HTTP/2 server sends against its reset budget
entries.body:
A client could make the server reset streams on its behalf — a malformed frame, a flow-control error, a refused stream — without spending its own reset budget, which is the MadeYouReset attack. Every RST_STREAM the server sends for a stream error or a refusal, and every 431, is now charged to the connection's reset credit like a client's reset, and a client that runs the credit out gets GOAWAY ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM. The public `reset()` an application calls stays uncharged. A finished response still earns a credit back, so the record (H2-4) states the sustained rate this leaves and the cost to a conforming client that draws many 431s on one connection.

Fixes #805
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: pin an unannotated secret(...) of a class written as a const alias or a call result
entries.body:
#771 made `const k = secret(v)` compile without a `Secret<T>` annotation, but for a class payload only the `secret(new C(...))` form had a golden. tests/cases/secret_inferred now also binds a class held in a `const` and a class answered by a call, reads each through `expose` and wipes it, so the inferred `Secret<Counter>` cannot regress for either form without the case failing to type-check or its IR golden changing.

Fixes #791

entries.title: reserve libm's C99/C23 names in c-symbols past LLVM 18's table
entries.body:
src/c-symbols.ts reserved only the library functions LLVM 18's target library info names, so a Nish function called `tgamma`, `erf`, `ilogb` or any other C99/C23 `<math.h>` or C99 `<complex.h>` name a later LLVM recognises was emitted under that name and could be replaced by the libm call at -O2. The whole C23 `<math.h>` and C99 `<complex.h>` function sets, with their `f`/`l` variants, are now reserved: a private function with such a name is renamed (`@tgamma$`), and an exported one is refused with NL3037, as the LLVM 18 names already were. The list's header says which sources it tracks and that a new C standard means re-reading its function index by hand.

Fixes #651

entries.title: bump the go_modules group across 2 directories with 3 updates
entries.body:
Bumps golang.org/x/crypto to v0.52.0 (and its golang.org/x/sys
dependency) in the crypto bench's aead and handshake Go twins. The new
x/crypto asks for Go 1.25, so the twins' go.mod files now say so.

The twins build with GOTOOLCHAIN=local, and the runner image ships Go
1.24, so CI's test job now installs Go 1.25 with actions/setup-go before
the crypto bench runs.

Go 1.25 also speeds up Go's portable (purego) X25519, which narrowed the
curves family's portable proof at x25519@32 to 1.09x on CI's runner,
under the 1.2x floor. The proof is now a list: x25519@32 first, then
p256-verify@64 for a column that comes up short there, where purego
takes 2.5x. bench/crypto/curves/README.md records the figures.
metrics: Go purego vs its assembly at x25519@32, 1.63x on Go 1.24.7, 1.23x on Go 1.25.1 (local), 1.09x on CI; at p256-verify@64, 2.49x on Go 1.25.1

entries.title: cap relay peers by a validated address only
entries.body:
The relay example counted a connection against its address's per-peer cap at the first Initial, before QUIC had validated that address, so Initials with a forged source address could take the places of a real client at that address. A peer now claims its place only once the slot's address is validated (a Retry or a Handshake packet from it), and std/net/http3-server.ts's doc comment says what `addressValidated` does and does not prove. The record states the trade-off this leaves: before validation an address is capped by nothing, so one non-spoofing address can hold unvalidated slots until `helloTimeout` where it was held to `maxPerPeer + spareSlots`; `retry: true` closes both holes at a round trip's cost.

Fixes #806

entries.title: print the noise band per crypto row and pin the --validate mismatch
entries.body:
bench/crypto now prints each row's noise band — the spread between nish and its byte-identical copy over the same interleaved rounds — beside the figure, so a delta can be read against its own noise. tests/run.js pins `--validate`: a temp copy of the curves family with one expected.txt checksum altered must exit 1 with the exact mismatch line, and the unaltered copy must pass.

The "portable columns are portable" gate failed other pull requests at random on curves' openssl-portable at x25519@32 (1.029-1.046x against a 1.05x floor), because OpenSSL runs nearly the same x25519 code with and without the asm mask. A twin listed in the family's new `portableRounds` field is now also proved by interleaved pairs: the portable column must be slower in at least 36 of 48 rounds (a false pass about 3.5e-4), re-measured once on a miss. Every other family and twin keeps its ratio floor.

Fixes #790

entries.title: correct the safegcd changelog's ct_asm claim and the off-main anchors in ct-verification.md
entries.body:
docs/security/ct-verification.md cited six commits that never landed on main — pre-squash branch commits of #537, #584, #594, #598 and #660 — so its anchors could not be checked out. Each now cites the squash commit on main that carries the same change, with line numbers re-read at that commit. The 0.19.0 release notes said the safegcd inversion's ct_asm fixture covered the normalisation; it covers one 30-divstep batch and both matrix updates, and the rest is held by discipline, as the fixture's header says. CHANGELOG.md renders only the subject, so it needed no change.

entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: accept a fresh parallelMapInto destination beside captured arrays
entries.body:
parallelMapInto refused a destination whenever the arrow also captured a fresh array or an object holding one, because it could not tell the two apart, so the programs in #612 did not compile even though nothing could alias. A destination that is a fresh `const` array, declared in the calling function and never handed on before the call — not stored, passed, aliased, captured, returned or written by an earlier parallelMapInto, and not handed on after the call inside a loop around it that it was declared outside of — is now known apart from every capture. Indexing it, reading `length`, calling its methods and iterating it with `for…of` do not hand it on. The host function is looked up in the call's own module only, so an imported function's offsets and node ids can never stand in for it. Every way in is pinned by a refusal test, each shown to compile once its condition is removed.

Fixes #612
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: close the lazy-slot acceptance gaps left after #786
entries.body:
The lazy-slot work left four acceptance gaps (#789). tests/run.js now holds the cost of building one Http3Server slot to exactly HTTP3_SERVER_SLOT_BYTES (111,568 bytes, measured by startup.ts), so a slot that keeps too much or too little fails; before, the figure appeared only in comments. net_http3_server checks that the first Initial into a never-built slot builds it and that a client taking a released slot keeps 0 bytes. net_http2_bad_config_tls drives Http2TlsServer's config validation and pins its panic message. The TLS, HTTP/3 and QUIC records now cite the merged commits (#767, #777, #779) and quote their checks verbatim.

Fixes #789
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: cache the test job's apt packages and bound each download
entries.body:
The `test` job's "Install LLVM 18 + lld (Ubuntu)" step hit its five-minute
limit on one shard of most main runs: the Azure mirror served valgrind,
libc6-dbg and the wasi packages (~23 MB; clang/lld/llvm 18 are already on the
image) at a trickle, never idle long enough for APT_OPTS's 30-second
connection timeout to fire.

The job now keeps those .debs in the Actions cache, keyed by runner image, so
a shard normally downloads nothing. The cache is saved right after the
install rather than at job end, so a red test still leaves it for the next
run. On a miss, each `--download-only` attempt is cut at one minute, and the
second and third attempts drop the Azure mirror from
/etc/apt/apt-mirrors.txt, since a retry against it stalls again.

entries.title: drop the PR body attribution check
entries.body:
The `PR body` workflow (`no attribution`) failed every pull request an agent
opened from a platform that appends its own footer to the body after the
pull request is created. Nothing in the session could remove that footer, so
the check could only be cleared by hand in the web editor and otherwise sat
red on every such pull request. It is removed, with `scripts/check-pr-body.mjs`
and its test.

The PreToolUse hook `.claude/hooks/no-attribution.mjs` stays: it still
refuses a tool call that would write attribution into a commit, a tag or a
pull request, and `npm test` still runs its suite.
entries.author: Amrit Kahlon

entries.title: use ECN counts in QUIC recovery
entries.body:
QUIC loss recovery now reads a peer's ACK_ECN counts. They are validated against the packets this side marked ECT(0) (RFC 9000 §13.4.2.1): a falling count, counts past the packets marked, a rise too small for the marked packets newly acknowledged, a plain ACK of a marked packet, or every testing packet lost fails the path, which is never marked again. A rise in ECN-CE on a validated path is a congestion event that halves the window once per recovery period, as a loss does (RFC 9002 §7.1, §B.7). A sent packet's mark lives in a spare bit of its existing state byte, so a built HTTP/3 slot grows by 120 bytes (HTTP3_SERVER_SLOT_BYTES 111,688).

Marking is opt-in (`ecnMarking`, off by default) because no carrier sets the IP ECN bits yet, so this is inert until http3-server.ts and quic-listener.ts are wired; the record (QUIC-10) is Partial until then.

Fixes #474

entries.title: decode HPACK into caller-owned storage and bound the HTTP/2 header bomb (#473)
entries.body:
An HTTP/2 connection now decodes header blocks into storage it owns and reuses. A small block can no longer expand about 1000:1 into fresh allocations (H2-1). The dynamic table keeps its entries in one byte store, decoded fields come from size-classed pools, and a field past the header-list limit is counted, never copied.

Every table copy is bounded per header block. A block may move at most 4 × max(table size, block length) octets through the table. Past that the connection ends with GOAWAY ENHANCE_YOUR_CALM, because the block is valid HPACK used as a lever.

Decoded fields, and any `u8[]` taken from them, are valid only until the next header block on the connection, for any stream. `conn.fields` is cleared before each decode, so a held request reads empty rather than another stream's octets. A program that needs a value later copies it; docs/guide/using-nish/http-router.md shows how.

Measured: 0 arena bytes for the last 50 of 101 bomb blocks of each kind; 728 → 0 bytes kept per request in the HTTP/2 TLS and loopback tests
Fixes #473

entries.title: publish to npm as nish instead of @amritk/nish
entries.body:
The unscoped npm name `nish` now belongs to this project, so the package moves to it: `npm install -g nish`. The per-platform binary packages keep their names, `@amritk/nish-<asset>`, and npm still installs the one for your machine alongside it. `bin/packaging.js` spells that prefix once, and the launcher, postinstall, the release workflow and the tests all read it from there. The release-PR bump now moves every pinned platform package rather than matching them by the main package's name.

The README and the installation guide lead with the install script, which needs neither Node nor npm, and give npm second.

entries.title: run an HTTP server on every core with a prefork supervisor (#478)
entries.body:
* feat(net): run an HTTP server on every core with a prefork supervisor (#478)

nish/net/prefork starts one worker process per core, each binding its own
SO_REUSEPORT listener, restarts a worker that dies (with a doubling backoff
for one that dies young), and stops them all on SIGTERM or SIGINT.
preforkWorkers(process.argv) answers a worker its index, and the supervisor
-1 once its workers are gone or -2 when one could not be started.
examples/prefork-server.ts is a whole server built on it, and
bench/http1-server.ts runs as BENCH_CORES workers under it.

Tests: tests/link/net_prefork, tests/link/net_prefork_bad_config

* docs(net): measure the prefork bench server at 1, 2 and 4 cores

bench/README.md records http1-server.ts under BENCH_CORES: keep-alive
plaintext rises 2.2x at 2 cores and post-json 3.7x at 4, while
Connection: close does not scale on a four-vCPU machine where wrk loses a
core to the server. The backoff's nested ternary becomes an if for lint.

Measured: plaintext keep-alive c=256 103,768 -> 224,012 req/s at 2 cores (band 8.4%)
Tests: tests/link/net_prefork

* build(self): ship nish/net/prefork in the std list and the release gates

The std module registry and release.yml's three presence gates name every
std file; net/prefork joins both so the package ships it.

* fix(net): keep a prefork supervisor running through failed restarts and foreign children

Review round 1 of the prefork supervisor. `stop` no longer returns when its
blocking reap collects a child that is not a worker: it reaps until every
worker is accounted for or no child is left. A restart that `spawn` refuses
waits on the same backoff as a worker that died young and is tried again;
only a worker's first start ends the supervisor with `PREFORK_SPAWN_FAILED`.
`backoffMs` must be above 0, since doubling 0 never reaches the cap.

The guide now says that `NISH_WORKERS` has no upper bound and is the
operator's to set, and that a supervisor killed by SIGKILL, the OOM killer,
SIGHUP or SIGQUIT leaves its workers running. The link test's workers end
their supervisor once the driver is gone, so a dead harness leaves nothing
restarting. The bench's workers check in with a two-byte index, and its
README gains the system-time and RSS columns its prose cites.

Tests: tests/link/net_prefork, tests/link/net_prefork_zero_backoff

* fix(net): reap through one path in prefork's SIGKILL phase and pin it

`stop`'s SIGKILL phase no longer blocks in `waitPid(-1, 0)` with its own
handling of a pid that is not a worker. It reaps through `reap(true)`, the
same path as the grace period, which skips a foreign pid. It waits a tick
between reaps and ends only when the last worker is reaped, or when
`waitPid` fails and so no child is left; `reap` now answers false in that
case. The branch the review asked to pin (a foreign pid returned by the
blocking wait) could only be reached when a foreign child died in the
microseconds between the last grace-period reap and the workers' SIGKILL
exits, so no test could reach it reliably. The branch is now gone instead of
kept untested.

tests/link/net_prefork step 7 (Linux) pins the shutdown with a non-worker
child. Its supervisor spawns a child of its own before `preforkWith`. The
two workers catch SIGTERM through `signalFd()` and never read it, so the
SIGKILL phase runs. The driver SIGTERMs the supervisor, then the foreign
child 200 ms into the 1 s grace period, so the child is reaped during
`stop`. `preforkWith` must return no sooner than the grace period. The
supervisor then lingers a second: an unreaped worker would still answer
`kill(pid, 0)` as a zombie, and none does.

The test was run against injected regressions in `stop`:
- A SIGKILL phase that does not reap fails, deterministically, with
  "worker N left behind" for both workers.
- A SIGKILL phase that reaps once and returns fails the same way.
- The pre-review blocking wait (returning on a foreign pid) passes, as does
  `reap` returning at a foreign pid. A foreign child that dies during the
  grace period is reaped there, and both bugs need it to die in the
  microsecond race above. With the restructure, a non-worker reap can no
  longer end the SIGKILL phase early.

Also from the review:
- When `signalFd`, `pollCreate` or `pollAdd` fails, `preforkWith` closes
  the loop it made. The signal pipe stays open: it is the process's one
  pipe, which every later `signalFd()` answers.
- The module doc, `PREFORK_SPAWN_FAILED`, the networking guide and the
  design note now say that -2 also covers "could not set up signal
  handling", with no worker started.
- The test's crash mode sets `quickExitMs` to 10 s, so a slow runner cannot
  turn a young crash into a reset backoff.

Tests: tests/link/net_prefork

* test(net): guard every pid the prefork test signals or waits on

The prefork link test now checks a pid is positive before it signals or
waits on it, and it never makes a blocking wait. A step whose supervisor
did not start, or whose children did not report, prints false and goes
no further.

`signal(pid, sig)` calls `kill` only for a positive pid. The runtime's
`kill` already refuses a pid of 0 or below with -EINVAL, so a bad pid
could not have signalled a process group. But step 7's `kill(foreign, 0)
!== 0` read that refusal as "reaped" and could pass when it should fail.

`exitsZero(pid, ms)` replaces each `waitPid(sup, 0)`. It is a WNOHANG loop
with a deadline, sends SIGKILL past the deadline, and never waits on a pid
that is not positive: `waitPid(-1, 0)` waits for any child and would have
blocked until the harness timed out.

Checked by a scratch copy whose `selfPath` names a missing file: `spawn`
answers -2, each step prints false and returns, and strace shows no
`kill` and no `wait4` from the test.

Tests: tests/link/net_prefork

entries.title: print each runner's CPU fingerprint and time a same-runner A/A pass
entries.body:
A constant-time timing reading now names the CPU it was taken on and carries
the false-positive rate of that machine, measured in the same job.
tests/ct-timing.js prints one fingerprint line before its table, read from
/proc/cpuinfo and sysfs: vendor, family, model, stepping, microcode and model
name on x86-64; implementer, part, variant, revision and MIDR_EL1 on aarch64,
with only the Neoverse parts that can be cited named; and the hypervisor
flag, the boost state and the kernel release. A field the kernel does not
give prints "unreadable", and a host without /proc/cpuinfo falls back to
os.cpus() and says so.

After the timing pass, every linked driver is run again under --null, with
the same re-measure rule, and the table gains an A/A column and a summary
line naming what crossed. The pass never changes the exit code. When it
crosses on a function the timing pass flagged, the summary says so. The
controls must still differ on their first measurement, and --no-aa leaves the
pass out. ct-timing.yml's report job puts each runner's fingerprint and A/A
line in the issue comment, and files an A/A crossing.

docs/security/ct-verification.md replaces the estimated runner rate with the
measured one and records what a same-machine null cannot do: it bounds false
alarms without making them zero, and it does not catch a weak leak, a CPU
never sampled, or an input no fixture uses.

Measured: aa_runs dispatch run 39733213208 (10 runs, head 6717ff9), 0 of 540 function-runs above |t| = 4.5 on an EPYC 9V74 and 0 of 540 on arm64; 0 of 940 earlier on a cloud VM; --quick here, 0 of 54 in the A/A pass
Refs #807

entries.title: Ed25519 signatures (RFC 8032) in std/crypto (#788)
entries.body:
* feat(std): Ed25519 signatures (RFC 8032) in std/crypto (#788)

`nish/crypto/ed25519` signs and verifies with Ed25519: `ed25519PublicKey(seed)`,
`ed25519Sign(seed, msg)` and `ed25519Verify(pub, msg, sig)`. The seed is a
`Secret<u8[]>`; key derivation and signing run inside `expose` and wipe the
seed hash, nonce, digits, points, scratch and both SHA-512 states before they
return. Scalar multiplication is constant time by discipline: signed radix-16
digits, a masked select over every table entry, complete twisted Edwards
formulas. Verification is variable time, cofactorless, and refuses S >= L,
non-canonical keys and keys off the curve.

The field arithmetic is X25519's, now exported from `nish/crypto/x25519`; the
shared part of the inversion chain is split out as `f25519Pow250` so Ed25519's
square root reuses it. The `curves` bench family gains sign and verify kernels.

Refs: docs/security/crypto-ecc.md (ECC-5)
Tests: tests/link/crypto_ed25519, tests/link/crypto_ed25519_f64

* fix(std): list nish/crypto/ed25519 among the std modules and release gates

A new std module is named in `src/std-modules.ts`, which the "not part of the
standard library" diagnostic lists, and in release.yml's three presence gates,
so a release cannot ship without it.

Tests: tests/run.js (std-modules list, release.yml presence gates)

* docs(security): code-span ECC-5's verification equation so it is not read as a link

* docs(security): word ECC-5's verification equation without link syntax

* fix(std): bound Ed25519 message length and pin more refusals

ed25519Sign and ed25519Verify now panic on a message longer than
2^31 - 1 bytes, as sha512 does. Under --number-mode f64 the length goes
through toI32, so both would otherwise hash a prefix, and a signature
would verify for any longer message sharing it. A 2 GiB test is
impractical, so tests/run.js reads each function's compare and panic in
the f64 IR. Deleting the verify guard fails the check.

tests/link/crypto_ed25519 adds the refusal of an S with bit 255 set, an
S of 2^253 or more, and an R with x = 0 and the sign bit set. It also
pins what cofactorless verification does with the order-2 key (0, -1):
R = the identity with S = 0 verifies when k is even and is refused when
k is odd. The module, ECC-5 and the guide say that small-order keys are
not refused.

ECC-5 records the length limit. It now presents the node:crypto
agreement run and the wipe-deletion run as one-off checks from
2026-10-22, not as standing evidence. ed25519 is added to the
crypto-ecc scope in docs/security/README.md, to std/README.md and to
docs/LANGUAGE.md's std/crypto lists.

Refs: docs/security/crypto-ecc.md#ECC-5
Tests: tests/link/crypto_ed25519
